A1.justification: Both PDFs describe ReSeek and FictionalHot. Their full text, equations, tables, figures, and appendices are readable, including image-based case studies. Retained material can be matched despite substantial reformatting and renumbering.

before.justification: v1 reports original ReSeek benchmark results, reranker and interaction-budget ablations, larger-model experiments, live-search evaluations, and case studies.

after.justification: v3 retains original experiments and adds component controls, sensitivity analyses, human dataset audits, training diagnostics, and repeated-run results.

M1.justification: Section 3.2 changes the specified self-correction procedure. v1 omits observations judged bad from the next context; v3 retains the action, observation, and judgment label, using semantic filtering instead. This substantively changes the information available to the policy after a negative judgment. The terminal answer reward was already depicted in v1 Figure 2.

E1.justification: The eight QA benchmarks and the live-search setting are retained. The reported FictionalHot seed-source coverage narrows from seven benchmarks in v1 Section 3.5 to six in v3, explicitly excluding Bamboogle. Bamboogle remains a standalone evaluation benchmark.

E2.justification: The comparator set is selectively updated: Table 3 removes SFT for both model sizes, while v3 Table 13 adds HiPRAG. Table 6 also introduces reranker-only and prompt-only controls without additional RL training. The other main baseline methods remain.

E3.justification: Appendix A.1 changes the stated learning rate from 1e-6 to 1e-5 and maximum turns from one to four, resolving the latter's disagreement with v1's main text without establishing that experiments were rerun. New protocols include threshold sweeps from 0.40 to 0.80, alternative penalty configurations, latency measurements through six turns, and two 500-instance dataset assessments.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained reranker, retriever, and turn ablations, v3 separately tests JUDGE and its reward, reranker-only versus RL-trained judgment, threshold sensitivity, and asymmetric penalties. It adds training-return and format-violation diagnostics, latency analysis, FictionalHot quality audits, and a retrieval-failure case. These address mechanism attribution, reliability, and failure conditions previously unexamined.

E5.justification: v1 provides no repeated-run uncertainty analysis. v3 Appendix A.10 first reports five independent training runs with named seeds, means and standard deviations, and paired t-test p-values; Tables 15 and 17 add ablation standard deviations. The significance-test comparator is inconsistent: the prose names Search-R1, whereas Table 14 displays ZeroSearch.

E6.justification: Retained Table 3 rows preserve their scores, but v3 adds substantial diagnostic and validation results, including the JUDGE-only average of 0.297 and FictionalHot novelty/consistency pass rates of 99.6%/99.2%. Existing results also change: Google-search FictionalHot scores fall from 0.055/0.059 to 0.003/0.003, and PPO-base FictionalHot scores change from 0.388/0.291 to 0.03/0.03. Several revised tables contain inconsistent averages, limiting quantitative interpretation.

T1.justification: Equation 2 undergoes a non-equivalent formal revision from indicator-based observation omission to concatenation of the action, observation, and judgment. This changes the mathematical context definition. Neither version contains theoretical guarantees or proofs; much of v3's additional reward mathematics explicitly documents previously described ingredients.

C1.justification: The central claims of self-correcting search, stronger QA performance, and contamination-resistant evaluation remain. v3 refines the claimed reward contribution into terminal answer correctness plus judgment supervision. It also drops v1's concluding proposal for the broader standardized Hot Benchmark protocol, narrowing the contribution framing.

C2.justification: New Section 5 identifies a substantive limitation: answer-conditioned rewards can undervalue intermediate bridge evidence in deep reasoning. New analyses interpret precision-oriented penalties, learned format adherence, and the four-turn efficiency tradeoff. The live-search discussion now attributes residual FictionalHot accuracy to guessing binary answers. Appendix A.12 additionally attributes failure to retrieval limits and argues against reward hacking, although those broad conclusions exceed the single case presented.

D1.justification: v3 supplies training-set provenance and counts, evaluation and FictionalHot composition, the specific bge-reranker-large model, reward constants, and a format-enforcement/retry mechanism. Appendix A.1 revises hardware from Ascend NPUs to H20 GPUs and updates learning-rate and turn settings. These materially expand reproducibility information. The homepage, code, dataset, and model resource links already existed in v1.

R1.justification: Sections 2.1–2.2 add explicit distinctions from MDBench, S2R, and AgentPRM. HiPRAG, FlashRAG, and the BGE resource reference are also newly cited. This updates relevant comparisons and attribution while retaining the established positioning around retrieval, search agents, and reinforcement learning.

P1.justification: The introduction, related work, methodology, and qualitative discussion receive extensive condensation and rewriting. The live-search analysis moves into the main experiments, dedicated Limitations and Impact Statement sections appear, and the appendix is reorganized around dataset documentation, diagnostics, statistics, and case studies. GRPO terminology and author/header information also change.

P2.justification: The main text changes from a single-column preprint layout to a two-column format. Figure 1 is redrawn vertically, Figure 3 corrects its fictional example, and substantial new tables and diagnostic plots are added. Existing live-search results move into the main text; the original four case-study figures are retained and relocated.

improvement.justification: The component controls, FictionalHot audits, clearer method specification, and explicit bridge-evidence limitation make important aspects of the work easier to assess than in v1. These benefits are tempered by new reporting inconsistencies: Table 7 retains old averages after changing scores, Table 14 conflicts with the stated significance-test comparator, and Appendix A.12 overgeneralizes from one failure case. The resulting net improvement is limited.
